title: The Lenz Lab
summary: Use Lenz’s law to find the direction of induced currents and the work done against them.
subject: physics
ncertRef: Section 6.5, Lenz’s law and conservation of energy
concepts: No change of flux, no emf
Work done against the induced current
learningOutcome: The student can use Lenz’s law to find the direction of an induced current for a magnet, a loop and a changing field, spot cases with no induced emf, and link the induced force to conservation of energy.

levels.title: Magnet and coil
levels.adds: Baseline: the induced current opposes the change in flux, so a coil repels an approaching magnet and attracts a receding one (Section 6.5).
hints: An approaching pole increases the flux through the coil, so the coil makes the same pole face it.
Use the right-hand rule to turn that pole into a direction of current.
The coil always opposes the motion, to conserve energy.

levels.title: Loop in a field
levels.adds: New idea: decide if the flux increases, decreases or stays the same, then oppose it (Ex 6.1, 6.2, Examples 6.4, 6.5).
hints: Moving out of a field, squeezing, or a fading field all decrease the flux.
The induced current makes a field in the same direction as the original to prop it up, or opposite to oppose an increase.
If the flux does not change, there is no current at all.

levels.title: Pulling a rod
levels.adds: More steps: the induced current feels a force opposing the motion, and the work done becomes heat (Section 6.5).
hints: The motional emf is Blv, and I = emf/R.
The force on the rod is BIl, opposing the motion.
The power supplied is F v, which equals I²R.

misconceptions: The induced current helps the change in flux
A strong magnetic field alone induces a current in a loop
A coil attracts an approaching magnet
